title: GeoGramBench: Benchmarking the Geometric Program Reasoning in Modern LLMs
claim: Adding procedural code to otherwise-textual problems consistently degrades accuracy across strong models, exposing a gap in program-based spatial reasoning.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right: example problem, then two bar charts with red drop arrows
description: Three panels in a row. The left panel shows a sample geometry problem about triangle ABC with an [asy] drawing-code block and the answer 54. A rounded dashed box on its right holds the rendered triangle diagram, labeled 'visualize'. The middle and right panels are grouped bar charts of accuracy for GPT-o1, R1, QwQ-32B and R1-Distillation-32B. Each model has three bars: all problems P in gray, text-only P_T in light orange, and text+code P_TC in light blue. Red downward arrows run from the orange bar to the blue bar, with red percentage-drop labels such as -24% and -38% on AIME24, and -9.9% to -13.7% on MATH-500. Subcaptions (a), (b), (c) sit below. The eye goes first to the code block, then to the red arrows.
caption: Overview and performance analysis on text-only (PT ) and text+code (PT C) geometry problems. (a) The procedural code is wrapped with [asy][/asy] and its geometric figure is visualized to facilitate understanding. (b) and (c) show accuracy comparisons of models on PT and PT C subsets in AIME24 (|PT C| = 5, |PT | = 25) and MATH-500 (|PT C| = 42, |PT | = 458), respectively. In both benchmarks, accuracy consistently drops for problems with procedural code.
abstract: Geometric spatial reasoning forms the foundation of many applications in artificial intelligence, yet the ability of large language models (LLMs) to operate over geometric spatial information expressed in procedural code remains underexplored. In this paper, we address this gap by formalizing the Program-to-Geometry task, which challenges models to translate programmatic drawing code into accurate and abstract geometric reasoning. To evaluate this capability, we present GeoGramBench, a benchmark of 500 carefully refined problems organized by a tailored three-level taxonomy that considers geometric complexity rather than traditional mathematical reasoning complexity. Our comprehensive evaluation of 17 frontier LLMs reveals consistent and pronounced deficiencies: even the most advanced models achieve less than 50% accuracy at the highest abstraction level. These results highlight the unique challenges posed by program-driven spatial reasoning and establish GeoGramBench as a valuable resource for advancing research in symbolic-to-spatial geometric reasoning. Project page: https://github.com/LiAuto-DSR/GeoGramBench.
